title: Checkpoint: Engines and Motion
objective: After this level you can explain how machines and engines turn energy into motion.
summary: One horsepower is about 746 watts. Engines turn heat into motion, motors turn electricity into motion, and levers, gears and hydraulics trade force for distance.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale: one horsepower is more than one horse can keep up.
cards.body: James Watt set the unit in the late 1700s, after experiments with strong dray horses. It came out about 50% more than an average horse can manage over a working day. Engines have been measured against horses ever since. Time to line up this chapter's machines.

cards.context: Watt defined it as 33,000 foot-pounds of work per minute. In Level 10's units, that's about 746 joules every second. So a 100-horsepower engine delivers about 74,600 watts, or about 75 kilowatts. Two units of power, both from the same man: one named for horses, one named for him.

mascot.line: Watt measured his engines in horses and got a unit named after himself. Excellent career move.

cards.headline: Engines and motion: three ways to move

items.label: Electricity into motion
points: A battery-powered motor turns the wheels (Level 25)
Braking can turn motion back into charge

items.label: Force traded for distance
points: A bigger piston, a bigger push (Level 28)

cards.headline: One rule under all of them
cards.body: No machine in this chapter makes energy. A gas engine turns fuel into motion but loses most of it as heat. An electric car loses far less, getting over 77% of its plug energy to the wheels. Levers, gears and hydraulics only reshape a push: more force, paid for with more distance. Horsepower and watts just measure how fast any of them delivers the energy.

questions.prompt: About how many watts is one horsepower?

options.label: About 100 watts
About 746 watts
About 1,000 watts
options.rationale: Close, but a horsepower is a bit less.

options.label: About 33,000 watts
options.rationale: 33,000 is foot-pounds per minute, not watts.

questions.explanation: One horsepower, 33,000 foot-pounds per minute, is about 746 watts.

questions.prompt: An engine is rated at 100 horsepower. About how much power is that in kilowatts?

options.label: About 1 kilowatt
About 7.5 kilowatts
About 75 kilowatts
About 746 kilowatts
options.rationale: That mixes up watts and kilowatts.

questions.explanation: 100 x 746 watts is about 74,600 watts, or about 75 kilowatts.

questions.prompt: Engines and Motion recap: how does a car engine use heat differently from Level 22's steam engines?

options.label: Its fuel burns inside the cylinder, not a boiler
It uses no heat at all, only moving air
options.rationale: Burning fuel makes the heat that drives it.

options.label: It relies on a vacuum made by a cold-water spray
It turns electricity straight into motion

questions.explanation: Steam engines made steam in a separate boiler; a car engine burns its fuel inside the cylinder itself.

questions.prompt: Engines and Motion recap: what do a pulley system, a pair of gears and a hydraulic lift have in common?

options.label: They all burn fuel to make their extra force
They all need electricity to run at all
options.rationale: All of them can work by hand.

options.label: They all create a little extra energy
They multiply force but cost extra distance

questions.explanation: Each one gives a bigger force in return for more rope, more turns or more piston travel. The energy stays the same.

questions.prompt: From Level 25: what does an electric car's motor do during regenerative braking?

options.label: It speeds up to cool down the friction brakes
options.rationale: It slows the car, not speeds it.

options.label: It acts as a generator, charging the battery
It switches off completely until you accelerate
options.rationale: It keeps working, as a generator.

options.label: It burns a little fuel to help the car slow

questions.explanation: The wheels spin the motor, which runs as a generator, sending electricity back into the battery as it slows the car.
